newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Canada willing to lead multi-nation force in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Canada willing to lead multi-nation force in Zaire.

text.p: Canada has offered to lead a multinational force to help end the refugee crisis in eastern Zaire, according to diplomatic sources at the United Nations.

They said the proposal had been made in an informal meeting on Monday by Canada's U.N. ambassador, Robert Fowler, thereby making the likelihood of a force more probable. Canadian officials however would not confirm the offer.
France, Spain, Mali and South Africa have pledged troops to an international force to help hundreds of thousands of refugees at risk of dying of hunger or thirst in eastern Zaire.

Sources at the United Nations said officials were still waiting to hear from the United States and Britain, with Washington expected to give its answer on troops to the Central African region before the end of the week.
"It still won't be enough," said one envoy of the Canadian offer. "We still need other contributors, notably the United States. I think the Canadians also want the Americans there."

Fowler and other Canadian diplomats could not be reached for comment. But in Ottawa, Captain Darryl Dubuc, duty officer at Canada's National Department of Defence, said the decision was not final. "There has been some contingency planning but nothing has been decided," he told Reuters.

At Canada's foreign ministry, spokesman John Bell said a decision had not been made yet. But he said Prime Minister Jean Chretien conferred by telephone with 15 world leaders during the weekend, urging them to support a force in Zaire.
"Prime Minister Chretien decided that the urgency of the situation required some action," Bell said.
Nevertheless, the U.N. sources said Canada had offered to make a "fairly substantial contribution". Precise figures were not yet available.
The U.N. Security Council early on Saturday asked members to lay the groundwork for such a force but did not authorise it until its aims and participation were clear.

The French government, which was the first to offer troops, said the force should be made up of 5,000 soldiers from numerous countries and stay no longer than two months. It would be organised and paid for by participating countries in an operation the Security Council would endorse.

However, the council delayed approval, mainly because of U.S. hesitations, and asked Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to draw up a "concept of operations and framework for a humanitarian task force" to get aid to more than one million refugees from ethnic violence in Rwanda and Burundi and to plan for their voluntary repatriation.
He is to report to the council by a Nov. 20 deadline. Diplomats said he could propose a U.N.-organised peacekeeping operation but only after the multinational force leaves.
But they said France would be unable to lead any force in the area because Tutsi-led Rwanda considered it an ally of the country's former Hutu-led government.

Refugee camps in eastern Zaire were created in 1994 after massacres of Tutsis by Hutus in Rwanda. During the turmoil that followed, French troops created a humanitarian zone that Rwanda claimed protected the perpetrators of genocide.

Canada recently fielded the U.N. special envoy for the Central African region, Raymond Chretien, its ambasador to Washington and nephew of Prime Minister Jean Chretien. He is currently in the area seeking support for such an intervention.

U.N. sources said Canada had hesitated at first because several of its French-speaking contingents were involved in the U.N. operation in Haiti. A Canadian general also led the ill-fated peacekeeping operation in Rwanda before and after the massacres there but Kigali officials were said to have thought well of the Canadian contingents.
